title: GOD TOLD ABRAHAM TO SEND THEM AWAY… SO WHY DID HE FOLLOW THEM INTO THE WILDERNESS?
paragraphs: GOD TOLD ABRAHAM TO SEND THEM AWAY… SO WHY DID HE FOLLOW THEM INTO THE WILDERNESS?
The heartbreaking story of Hagar and Ishmael reveals something many wounded believers have never understood: being sent away by people does not mean you have been abandoned by God.
She was carrying a dying child through the wilderness. The water was gone. Her strength was disappearing. And the family that should have protected her was now somewhere behind her.
But perhaps the most disturbing part of this story is not that Abraham sent Hagar and Ishmael away.
It is that God told Abraham to listen to Sarah.
And then, when the boy was crying in the wilderness, God heard him.
Why would the same God who permitted their departure promise to protect them?
Why would God allow a mother and her son to enter a wilderness where they could die?
And what does this reveal about the God we worship when obedience, human failure, rejection, and divine mercy collide?
Before we answer, there is something you need to know.
The Bible never tells us that Hagar was worthless. It never says Ishmael was forgotten. And it never presents their suffering as proof that God had stopped caring.

In fact, the most astonishing part of this account may be that while Abraham's household was celebrating the child of promise, God was listening to another child crying where nobody else could hear him.
And that changes how we should read the entire story.
Genesis 21:8–21 is not merely about a family separation.
It is about the painful consequences of human decisions, the unbreakable faithfulness of God's covenant, and the mercy of a God who sees people others have pushed aside.
And somewhere in this ancient wilderness, you may recognize your own story.
Because not everyone who has been abandoned did something to deserve it.
Not everyone who ends up in the wilderness chose to go there.
And not everyone who has been wounded by someone associated with God's promises has been rejected by God Himself.
Sometimes the people who should have protected you become part of the reason you are hurting.
Hagar knew that pain.
But to understand why God allowed this separation, we must return to the scandal that began long before the wilderness.
God had promised Abraham descendants, even though Abraham and Sarah had grown old without having a child together.
In Genesis 15:4–5, God promised Abraham that his own offspring would inherit his household and that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars.
But waiting exposed something deeply human.
Abraham believed God, yet his household struggled with the passing years.
Sarah was unable to conceive, and in Genesis 16, she gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham so that a child might come through her.
This arrangement reflected ancient social practices, but the fact that Scripture records a practice does not mean Scripture endorses its injustice.
Hagar was not an equal participant negotiating her future with Abraham and Sarah.
She was an enslaved Egyptian woman living under their authority.
That matters.
Because when we romanticize the story, we risk overlooking the vulnerability of the woman at its center.
Abraham fathered a child with Hagar.
His name was Ishmael.
And immediately, the household became fractured by jealousy, contempt, resentment, and mistreatment.
Sarah dealt harshly with Hagar, and Hagar fled into the wilderness.
There, in Genesis 16, the angel of the LORD found her beside a spring.
Notice that.
Before Hagar ever became the mother of a great nation, before she had anything impressive to offer, before she could establish herself in the world, God met her in her distress.
She was a servant.
A foreigner.
A pregnant woman.
A person with little power over the circumstances that had brought her suffering.
Yet heaven did not overlook her.
In Genesis 16:13, Hagar called upon the LORD who had spoken to her.
The Hebrew expression is:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי — Attah El Ro'i
Commonly understood as, “You are a God of seeing,” or “You are the God who sees me.”
The precise nuance of the Hebrew has been discussed by translators, but the central truth of the passage is unmistakable.
God had seen Hagar in her affliction.
He had not confused her low position in Abraham's household with low worth before Him.
And He had given her son a name before he was born.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma'el.
Ishmael.
The name means “God hears.”
Genesis 16:11 explains the reason: the LORD had heard Hagar's affliction.
Think about that.
Long before the boy cried beneath a bush in Genesis 21, his very name testified that God hears suffering.
His mother had already learned that God sees.
And together, their story carried two truths into the wilderness.
God sees.
God hears.
But if God saw Hagar and heard her suffering, why did He allow her to be sent away again?
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Years passed.
God fulfilled His promise to Sarah.
Isaac was born.
His name, יִצְחָק (Yitschaq), is associated with laughter, a fitting name after the astonishment and joy surrounding his promised birth.
The child Abraham and Sarah had waited for was finally in their arms.
The impossible had happened.
The household celebrated.
But underneath that celebration, the unresolved wounds of earlier decisions had not disappeared.
Genesis 21:9 tells us that Sarah saw Ishmael engaging in behavior described by the Hebrew word מְצַחֵק — metsacheq, a form of the verb associated with laughing or playing.
Some translations render the action as mocking.
Others use language such as laughing or playing.

The precise nature of Ishmael's behavior is debated. Galatians 4:29 later describes the relationship in terms of persecution, but Genesis 21:9 itself does not give a detailed account of what Ishmael did.
We should not invent details that Scripture does not supply.
What Scripture clearly tells us is Sarah's response.
She demanded that Abraham drive out Hagar and her son, insisting that Ishmael must not share the inheritance with Isaac.
Those words were not merely an expression of frustration.
They threatened the security and future of a mother and her child.
Abraham was deeply distressed.
Genesis 21:11 says the matter was grievous to him because Ishmael was his son.
And then God spoke.
Genesis 21:12, in the King James Version, records:
“Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice; for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.”
Here is the difficult truth.
God instructed Abraham to listen to Sarah regarding the separation, but that does not mean God approved every motive, attitude, or act of mistreatment within the household.
God's instruction concerned the covenantal future He had established through Isaac.
The promised covenant line would continue through Isaac, not Ishmael.
But God did not stop speaking there.
In Genesis 21:13, He promised that Ishmael would also become a nation because he was Abraham's offspring.
That second promise is essential.
Without it, we might misunderstand the entire event.
God was not telling Abraham that Ishmael had no value.
He was distinguishing between the particular covenant promise entrusted to Isaac and His continuing care and purposes for Ishmael.
Isaac was the chosen heir of the covenant promise. Ishmael was still a son whom God heard, preserved, and blessed.
Those two truths are not contradictions.
They belong together.
God's election of Isaac did not require God to despise Ishmael.
And God's care for Ishmael did not overturn His covenant with Isaac.
Scripture can affirm both without diminishing either.
This is where we must be careful.
Some people read the account as though God simply approved Sarah's cruelty.
Others try to soften the story until the injustice disappears.
Neither approach does justice to the text.
The passage is painfully honest about the consequences of a fractured household. It also reveals that God's faithfulness can continue amid circumstances shaped by human failure.
God's promises do not make human sin harmless.
And human sin does not make God's promises unreliable.
Early the next morning, Abraham gave Hagar bread and a container of water and sent her away with Ishmael.
The Bible does not describe a grand farewell.
No celebration.
No assurance from Abraham recorded in the passage.
Just provisions for the journey and a mother departing with her son.
She wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
And eventually, the water ran out.
Try to imagine that moment.
Not as a Bible illustration.
Not as a scene you already know will end well.
Imagine being the mother who does not know what happens next.
The sun is relentless.
Your child is weakening.
You search the container again, though you already know it is empty.
You look across the wilderness for something that resembles water.
Nothing.
You listen for footsteps.
Nothing.
And the worst possibility begins to settle into your chest.
Your child may die before you do.
Genesis 21:15–16 describes Hagar placing the boy beneath one of the shrubs and moving away because she could not bear to watch him die.
Then she wept.
The Hebrew text uses the language of lifting up her voice and weeping.
This was not a quiet moment of religious reflection.
This was a mother overwhelmed by the possibility of losing her child.
And there is something devastating about the fact that Hagar had already experienced God's intervention years earlier.
She knew what it meant to encounter the God who sees.
Yet here she was again.
In another wilderness.
Facing another crisis.
With no visible solution.
Have you ever been there?
Not necessarily in a desert.
Maybe in a hospital corridor where the doctor said something you were not prepared to hear.
Maybe at the kitchen table, staring at bills you could not pay.
Maybe inside a marriage where the person who promised to stay had already emotionally left.
Maybe after a betrayal by someone you trusted.
Maybe in a church where you expected compassion but experienced humiliation instead.
You remembered the prayers God had answered before.
You remembered the Scriptures that once gave you strength.
You remembered telling other people to trust Him.
But now it was your turn to sit beneath the weight of something you could not fix.
And the question came.
“Lord, if You see me, why am I here again?”
Hagar's story does not give us permission to promise that every painful situation will end exactly as we want.
It does give us a reason to reject the lie that suffering proves God has forgotten us.
Because what happened next is one of the most tender moments in Genesis.
Genesis 21:17 says:
“And God heard the voice of the lad.”
In Hebrew:
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר
Vayyishma Elohim et-qol hanna'ar.
Literally, “And God heard the voice of the boy.”
There it is.
The name Ishmael had carried from before his birth was becoming visible in the story again.
God hears.
And God heard him.
The text does not tell us exactly what the boy said or what form his crying took.
It simply tells us that God heard his voice.
Then the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven.
“What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.” (Genesis 21:17, KJV)
Read that last phrase again.
Where he is.
Not where he should have been.
Not where Sarah wanted him.
Not where Abraham could see him.
Where he was.
God knew his location.
God knew his condition.
God knew his need.
The boy was not outside the reach of divine mercy simply because he was outside Abraham's household.
And Hagar was not invisible simply because she had lost the protection and position she once knew.
The angel told her to rise, lift up the boy, and hold him by the hand, because God would make him into a great nation.
Then Genesis 21:19 says something extraordinary.
“And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.”
The Hebrew begins:
וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ
Vayyifqach Elohim et-eineha.
“And God opened her eyes.”
The text does not explain whether the well had been present but unnoticed, or whether God had provided it in a way the narrative does not describe.
We should not claim certainty where Scripture is silent.
But the result is clear.
Hagar saw the water.
She filled the container.
And she gave the boy a drink.
The child she feared she would watch die was given water to live.
What an extraordinary contrast.
The mother who had moved away because she could not bear to watch death now had a reason to move toward her son again.
The wilderness had not disappeared.
But provision had appeared within it.
And this is where the passage speaks so deeply to wounded people.
Sometimes we want God to explain every reason we were brought into a painful place.
Sometimes we want Him to reverse every decision someone made against us.
Sometimes we want the people who hurt us to acknowledge what they did.
And those desires can be understandable.
But Genesis 21 does not tell us that Sarah apologized.
It does not record Abraham coming to retrieve Hagar.
It does not say that the family was reunited.
What it tells us is that God heard, spoke, provided, and remained with the boy.
Genesis 21:20 says:
“And God was with the lad.”
Do not rush past that sentence.
The same boy whose inheritance would not be joined to Isaac's was not abandoned to a meaningless future.
God was with him.
Ishmael grew up in the wilderness, became an archer, and eventually lived in the wilderness of Paran. His mother obtained a wife for him from Egypt.
The story does not end with Ishmael becoming the covenant heir.
It ends with the fulfillment of God's promise that he would survive and have a future.
And Genesis 25 later records Ishmael's descendants, including twelve princes, consistent with the promise God had already made in Genesis 17:20.
God had not forgotten what He said.
Now consider something else.
The God who heard Ishmael in the wilderness is the same God whose saving purposes ultimately unfold through the promised line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, leading to Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1 begins by identifying Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
Galatians 3:16 places Christ at the center of the fulfillment of the Abrahamic promise.
This does not mean Hagar and Ishmael were merely disposable characters in someone else's story.
They were real people whose suffering mattered to God.
But it does mean their story belongs within a much larger biblical account of promise, human failure, mercy, and redemption.
And in Jesus Christ, we see God's mercy revealed with a fullness that should humble every one of us.
Jesus entered a world filled with rejection, injustice, and broken relationships.
He was despised and rejected by men, as Isaiah 53:3 prophetically describes the suffering servant.
He knew betrayal.
He knew abandonment.
He knew what it meant for those closest to Him to scatter when suffering came.
And at the cross, He bore our sins, accomplishing the redemption that no human effort could earn.
Yet we must not confuse the two stories.
Hagar's wilderness experience is not a direct prophecy of the crucifixion.
Ishmael is not presented in Genesis 21 as a substitute for Christ.
The connection is found in the consistent revelation of God's character and in the larger unfolding of His redemptive plan.
The God who did not ignore the cries of a vulnerable child is the God who, in Christ, reveals the depth of His compassion toward sinners.
And Jesus does more than offer temporary relief from distress.
He calls us to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He reconciles sinners to God through His death and resurrection.
He gives new life to those who trust in Him.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message about surviving difficult circumstances.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And that includes people who have been wounded by others.
It also includes people who have wounded others.
Perhaps you identify with Hagar.
You were treated as though your value depended on what you could provide.
You were useful until you became inconvenient.
You were included until someone decided you no longer belonged.
And you have spent years wondering whether the rejection of people reflects the judgment of God.
It does not necessarily.
People can reject someone whom God still sees with compassion.
But perhaps you identify more closely with Abraham.
You have made decisions that left someone else carrying pain.
You have allowed fear, passivity, or divided loyalties to damage relationships.
You may have believed that because God was still working in your life, the wounds caused by your choices no longer mattered.
They do.
God's faithfulness is never an excuse to avoid responsibility.
Or perhaps you recognize something of Sarah.
You have been so afraid of losing what God promised that you began treating another person as a threat.
You allowed insecurity to harden into resentment.
You wanted control more than you wanted compassion.
And somewhere along the way, protecting your own interests became more important than loving your neighbor.
If that is you, the answer is not to defend your sin by pointing to God's sovereignty.
The answer is repentance.
Because the Gospel does not merely comfort the wounded.
It also confronts the sinner.
And every one of us needs both mercy and truth.
Jesus did not come to tell us that our motives are always pure or that our decisions never harm others.
He came to save us from sin and transform us by His grace.
That is the beauty of redemption.
We do not have to pretend our past was righteous in order to believe God can redeem our future.
We do not have to rename cruelty as obedience.
We do not have to call abandonment love.
And we do not have to imagine that God's promises are dependent on human beings behaving perfectly.
If they were, none of us would have hope.
The story of Abraham's household is filled with extraordinary promises and deeply flawed people.
Yet God remained faithful.
Not because their actions were always admirable.
But because His character is faithful.
And that brings us to one of the most important distinctions in the entire passage.
Being outside a particular covenant role is not the same as being outside God's concern.
Isaac had a unique place in the unfolding covenant promise.
Ishmael did not occupy that same place.
But God still heard Ishmael, provided for him, and fulfilled His word concerning him.
This should destroy the arrogance that sometimes creeps into religious communities.
We must never confuse being entrusted with God's truth with being authorized to treat other people as worthless.
We must never use divine election as permission for human cruelty.
And we must never assume that someone outside our circle is beyond the reach of God's mercy.
If anything, those who have received grace should become more humble, more compassionate, and more serious about reflecting the character of Christ.
There is another truth here that may be difficult to accept.
God did not remove every consequence of the decisions made in Abraham's household.
Hagar and Ishmael still left.
Their lives still changed.
The family remained divided.
Divine provision did not erase the painful history.

And this is important because some Christians have been taught to expect that if God truly loves them, He will restore every relationship, reverse every loss, and return everything to the way it was before.
Scripture does not make that promise.
Sometimes reconciliation happens.
Sometimes it does not.
Sometimes God restores what was lost.
Sometimes He leads us into a future that looks nothing like the one we expected.
But the Christian hope rests on something deeper than a guaranteed return to former circumstances.
It rests on the living Christ.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
The One whose resurrection assures us that suffering and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So if you are in a wilderness season, do not build your faith on the expectation that God must bring back every person who walked away.
Build your faith on Jesus Christ.
Seek His wisdom.
Obey His Word.
Bring your grief before Him.
And where you have sinned, repent without excuses.
Where others have sinned against you, remember that forgiveness does not require pretending the wrongdoing was acceptable or returning to an unsafe situation.
God's mercy is not a command to deny reality.
It is an invitation to trust Him within reality.
And perhaps the most personal question in this story is not simply why Hagar and Ishmael were sent away.
Perhaps it is this:
What do you believe about God when the people you expected to stay are gone?
Do you believe His compassion ended when their support ended?
Do you believe your life has no purpose because someone else no longer sees a place for you?
Do you believe your tears are meaningless because no human being has responded?
Listen carefully.
Genesis 21 does not promise that every wilderness contains an immediately visible well.
But it does reveal a God who hears suffering, remembers His word, and is not limited by the boundaries people draw around their lives.
And the Gospel gives us an even greater assurance.
Romans 8:32 declares that God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.
Romans 8:38–39 assures believers that nothing in all creation can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the permanence of human approval.
Not in the certainty of comfortable circumstances.
Not in our ability to understand every painful event.
In Jesus.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The faithful Redeemer.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And maybe that is what you need to hear tonight.
You may not receive an explanation for every door that closed.
You may never hear an apology from everyone who wounded you.
You may not understand why God permitted a particular season of loss.
But you can come to Christ without pretending you are strong.
You can confess the bitterness you have carried.
You can surrender the desire to control every outcome.
You can ask Him to teach you to forgive without denying the truth.
And you can trust Him with the future you cannot yet see.
Because Christianity is not the promise that we will never cry in the wilderness.
It is the proclamation that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that those who belong to Him have a hope that reaches beyond every wilderness this life can bring.
That is not sentimental comfort.
That is resurrection hope.
And it is worth building your life upon.
If this story exposed something you have been hiding, do not rush away from it.
Maybe you need to repent for how you have treated someone.
Maybe you need to stop interpreting another person's rejection as God's rejection.
Maybe you need to return to prayer after months of silence.
Maybe you need to tell someone that you are struggling instead of pretending you are fine.
Or maybe, for the first time, you need to surrender your life to Jesus Christ.
You can begin right where you are.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned, and I need Your mercy. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to trust You. Heal what is broken in me, confront what is sinful in me, and lead me in Your truth. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magic formula. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, not earned through particular words, religious performance, or financial contributions.
But if those words express the genuine repentance and faith of your heart, do not dismiss this moment.
Turn to Christ.
And keep walking with Him.
I also want to ask you something personal.
Have you ever experienced a season when someone walked away, and you struggled to believe God still cared?
You do not have to share private details.
And if this passage has confronted something in your heart that needs repentance, you can simply write “Jesus, change my heart.”
And if someone comes into these comments carrying grief, please respond with compassion rather than judgment.
We are not here to compete over whose pain is greatest.
We are here to point one another to Christ.
Not because every difficult question has now been answered, but because Genesis 21 deserves to be revisited slowly, with an open Bible and a prayerful heart.
Someone among your friends may be silently wrestling with abandonment, disappointment, or the fear that God has forgotten them.
You may never know who reads it at the exact moment they need to be reminded of the Gospel.
We want believers to grow deeper in the Word, struggling Christians to find sound encouragement, and seekers to encounter the truth of the Gospel.
We believe biblical nourishment should be accessible to people who cannot afford expensive resources.
And we want that work to continue reaching more lives.
It is one practical way to participate in making these resources available to others.

Scripture teaches believers to give willingly and generously in support of good works and Gospel ministry. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So let me be clear about something important.
Christ has already accomplished what no financial contribution could ever accomplish.
Your salvation is not for sale.
Your worth before God is not measured by a monthly payment.
And your giving to your local church, your responsibilities to your family, and your care for people in need should never be neglected because of an online ministry.

Some believers may prayerfully view such recurring support as part of their broader giving or offerings. It should not automatically be treated as a substitute for whatever tithing or local-church commitments they hold.
These items are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith-centered reading, reflection, and conversation while helping sustain the work.
You can still be part of this mission.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and study the Scriptures we share.
Use the free resources.
And continue pointing people toward Jesus.
A single thoughtful share may introduce someone to a biblical truth they have never understood.
A sincere comment may encourage a person who feels alone.
A faithful prayer matters even when nobody else sees it.
Whatever you choose, let it be done for the glory of God, not out of guilt or pressure.
Because this ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And if Gospel Warrior ever succeeds in helping people become more impressed with the ministry than with Christ, then we will have missed the very purpose for which this work exists.
Our calling is to make Him known.
To open the Scriptures faithfully.
To speak truth with compassion.
To call sinners to repentance.
To proclaim forgiveness through the cross.
To remind wounded people that human rejection is not the final authority over their lives.
And to encourage believers to follow Jesus long after they have finished reading an article.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that wilderness.
A mother is sitting at a distance.
Her child is beneath a shrub.
The water is gone.
Her hope is fading.
She cannot bear to watch what she believes is coming.
But the story does not end where her strength ends.
God hears the boy.
God speaks to the mother.
Her eyes are opened.
Water is found.
And the child lives.
Not because Hagar had earned divine attention.
Not because Ishmael had inherited Isaac's covenant role.
Not because Abraham's household had handled everything perfectly.
But because God was faithful to His word.
And through the greater story of Scripture, that same faithfulness leads us to Jesus Christ, in whom God's saving promises find their fulfillment.
So when you remember Hagar, do not remember only the woman who was sent away.
Remember the God who saw her.
When you remember Ishmael, do not remember only the son who did not inherit Isaac's covenant place.
Remember the God who heard him.
And when you remember your own failures, wounds, regrets, and wilderness seasons, do not let them become the final definition of your life.
Bring them to Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not the claim that your story has never been painful.
It is the good news that your sin does not have to be your master, your wounds do not have to become your identity, and death does not have to be your final destination.
In Christ there is forgiveness.
In Christ there is redemption.
In Christ there is new life.
And in Christ there is a hope that cannot be extinguished by the wilderness.
The world may remember the day you were sent away, but never forget the God who heard your cry where you were.
